A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RM-R1, with matching authors, training framework, model families, and benchmarks. Their complete main texts and appendices, including tables, figures, equations, and proofs, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original RM-R1 evaluations on RewardBench, RM-Bench, and RMB, together with training ablations, scaling experiments, training dynamics, and a qualitative case study.

after.justification: v4 retains those original empirical results and reports revised ablation outcomes and additional baseline comparisons.

M1.justification: The substantive procedure remains reasoning-trace distillation followed by GRPO/RLVR, with chat-versus-reasoning CoR branches and a correctness reward. The distillation equation now appends the preference label rather than the preferred response, aligning it with the label-output prompts already in v1; this does not establish an implemented method change. The new rubric-free prompt is an ablation control.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same cleaned Skywork preference data, Code-Preference-Pairs, and Math-DPO-10K, and evaluate on RewardBench, RM-Bench, and RMB. Their represented domains and tasks remain unchanged. The added controls and theoretical discussion introduce no new evaluated task or dataset.

E2.justification: v4 substantially expands comparator coverage within the existing benchmarks. Examples include INF-ORM-Llama3.1-70B and JudgeLRM, additional InternLM2 and Skywork models on RewardBench, and GPT-4o, Gemini, Claude, and Self-taught Evaluator on RM-Bench. These are reported comparisons in Tables 1 and 6–8, not merely new citations. Self-taught Evaluator's category reassignment alone is not an addition.

E3.justification: v1's Cold Start RL already uses rubrics; v4 retains this as the '+ Rubrics' setting and adds a genuinely rubric-free control with a separate prompt. The model-size analysis also changes its description of improvement from absolute to relative. Main training budgets, model sizes, dataset sizes, and benchmark protocols otherwise remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 Table 2 adds a control that separates the contribution of rubric generation from query categorization, refining v1 Table 4's training-recipe ablation. The scaling studies, reasoning-versus-SFT comparisons, training dynamics, and sickle-cell case study are retained. Appendix J discusses computational overhead without adding measured latency or robustness experiments.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run estimates, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The retained GRPO reward normalization and v4's theoretical sampling probabilities do not constitute empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: RM-R1-Qwen-Instruct-32B's RewardBench total changes from 92.9 to 91.4 despite unchanged category scores, and its three-benchmark average changes from 81.7 to 81.2. Ablation results and the model-size scaling plot also change. Numerous baseline results are added: RM-Bench's strongest reported comparator rises from 70.1 to 75.2 while RM-R1's 83.9 remains unchanged, narrowing the comparison margin from 13.8 to 8.7 points.

T1.justification: New Appendix K introduces formal assumptions about high-reward filtering and feature disagreement, a lemma, a proposition comparing robust and shortcut policies under SFT and RL distributions, and complete proofs. v1 contains learning-objective equations but no corresponding theoretical analysis. v4 also corrects the formal distillation target.

C1.justification: The central reasoning-based reward-modeling and two-stage training contributions remain. Performance claims are recalibrated: v1 emphasizes gains up to 13.8% and generative-model leadership on RewardBench, whereas v4 emphasizes superiority averaged across three benchmarks and gains up to 4.9%. This changes the scope of the headline comparison without redefining the main research contribution.

C2.justification: v4 adds a substantive explanation linking filtered SFT data to shortcut retention and broader RL exploration to stronger incentives for robust behavior (Appendix K). Appendix J newly discusses reasoning latency and potential mitigation through overlapping rollout and reward computation. It also flags possible baseline contamination in Table 6 and emphasizes that RewardBench leadership need not transfer across benchmarks. The latency mitigation remains an argument, not a measured finding.

D1.justification: The new reproducibility statement describes repository contents, evaluation scripts, prompt/configuration files, and model-version recording beyond v1's general release announcement. v4 also supplies the new rubric-free control prompt. Most concrete training, hardware, and data-processing details already appeared in v1 and are retained in Appendices F and G.

R1.justification: The main related-work discussion and positioning against DeepSeek-GRM and JudgeLRM are retained in Appendix B. v4 adds references supporting cognitive motivation, SFT-versus-RL generalization, reasoning expressivity, and rubric applications, and expands baseline attribution. These are limited extensions of positioning; publication updates to existing references are not new works.

P1.justification: v4 extensively condenses and reorganizes the narrative: related work, detailed experimental setup, GRPO exposition, and ablation specifications move into appendices; training-recipe analysis precedes scaling; and the introduction and main-results discussion are rewritten. It also adds reproducibility and ethics statements and an appendix contents page, while removing the boxed takeaways.

P2.justification: v4 introduces a cross-benchmark summary table and relocates the expanded benchmark tables to the appendix. It places the scaling figure beside the SFT comparison table, compresses prompt displays, adds the rubric-free prompt figure, and splits the case-study presentation into a shortened main table and fuller appendix displays. Conference formatting changes the layout throughout.

improvement.justification: Expanded strong-baseline comparisons, correction of the 92.9 RewardBench total to 91.4, and the separate rubric-free control improve the credibility and interpretability of the evidence. The gains are limited by new reporting inconsistencies, including JudgeLRM's impossible 766.2 accuracy in Table 7 and mismatched summary/detail scores for Self-taught Evaluator. The added theory is conditional, and computational-overhead claims remain unmeasured.
